vt.analysis:
Type: OpenClaw Skill
Name: clawtoclaw
Version: 1.0.13

The OpenClaw AgentSkills bundle 'clawtoclaw' is designed for secure agent-to-agent coordination, including messaging and event management, with a strong emphasis on human approval and end-to-end encryption. The `SKILL.md` documentation explicitly guides the AI agent on security best practices, warning against prompt injection from other agents, unauthorized data sharing (e.g., calendars, credentials, private conversations), and treating decrypted messages as untrusted. Python scripts handle key generation, encryption, decryption, and event heartbeats, consistently interacting with the `clawtoclaw.com` API and storing sensitive data (API keys, private keys) in designated `~/.c2c/` paths with appropriate permissions. There is no evidence of intentional malicious behavior such as data exfiltration to unauthorized endpoints, unauthorized command execution, persistence mechanisms, or obfuscation. All network calls are directed to the stated service, and file system access is limited to the skill's operational needs.

llm.summary: The skill is mostly coherent with its coordination purpose, but it includes optional automated actions (a heartbeat that can auto-propose intros) and plaintext local credential handling that conflict with the SKILL.md's emphasis on keeping humans in control — review how it's run and where credentials/keys are stored before installing.

dimensions.detail: Name/description (coordinate with other agents) matches the provided code and instructions: API calls to https://www.clawtoclaw.com/api, keypair generation, encrypt/decrypt helpers, event state/heartbeat for check-ins and intros. No unrelated cloud credentials or binaries are requested.
dimensions.label: Purpose & Capability
dimensions.name: purpose_capability

dimensions.detail: Instructions and shipped scripts read and write local files (~/.c2c/credentials.json, ~/.c2c/keys/, ~/.c2c/active_event.json) and make network calls only to the declared API base. That is expected, but the event_heartbeat.py script supports an optional --propose mode that will automatically call events:proposeIntro (mutating the remote service) based on suggestion scores. SKILL.md repeatedly emphasizes 'human approval gates', while the example heartbeat invocation and the shipped runner encourage scheduled auto-proposal — a behavioral mismatch that could lead to the agent making commitments without manual approval if run with those flags or scheduled by the user.
dimensions.label: Instruction Scope
dimensions.name: instruction_scope

dimensions.detail: There is no install spec (instruction-only plus Python helper scripts). Shipped scripts use standard Python libraries plus PyNaCl (not bundled); the README mentions pip install pynacl. No remote downloads or obscure install sources are used.
dimensions.label: Install Mechanism
dimensions.name: install_mechanism

dimensions.detail: The skill requests no environment variables and no external credentials beyond an API key for clawtoclaw (stored in ~/.c2c/credentials.json). This is proportionate to the stated purpose. Note: credentials are stored/read as plaintext files; generate_keypair sets 0o600 on the key file but credentials.json is not automatically permissioned — users should ensure appropriate file permissions and secrets handling.
dimensions.label: Credentials
dimensions.name: environment_proportionality

dimensions.detail: always:false and user-invocable:true. The skill does not request forced inclusion or modify other skills. The only persistence is local state and keys under ~/.c2c, which is appropriate for the use case.
dimensions.label: Persistence & Privilege
dimensions.name: persistence_privilege

llm.guidance:
This skill's code and docs line up with its coordination purpose, but pay attention to two practical risks before installing:

- Automated actions: The heartbeat runner can be run with --propose (and examples recommend scheduling it). That will autonomously call events:proposeIntro on the remote API and could make introductions without human confirmation. If you want humans always in the loop, do not schedule/run the heartbeat with --propose or use --dry-run for testing.

- Local secrets and keys: The workflow asks you to save your raw API key and private key under ~/.c2c. Keep those files private (restrict permissions, consider storing in an OS secret store), and rotate the API key if you suspect compromise. generate_keypair writes keys with restrictive perms but credentials.json handling is explicit and may be plaintext.

- Review cron/automation: If you enable a scheduled runner (cron/systemd), double-check the exact command-line flags used so you don't accidentally enable mutating behavior.

- Verify the endpoint and trust: All network traffic goes to https://www.clawtoclaw.com/api. Only proceed if you trust that service and its privacy/security practices.

Overall: the skill appears functionally consistent, but the optional autonomous mutation capability (auto-propose) combined with plaintext local credentials is the main thing to watch — treat this as an operational/configuration risk rather than code that is obviously malicious.
